## When Coordination Became Programmable

Role prompts made multi-agent systems easy to imagine, but not easy to control. Once agents could use tools, write files, execute code, browse websites, update memory, and hand work to one another, the key design object was no longer only the prompt. It was the coordination substrate around the model: what state persists, what tools are callable, what actions are sandboxed, what logs survive, what artifacts are produced, who can route work, and how success is checked. AutoGen, AgentVerse, AgentScope, Magentic-One, OpenHands, AutoAgent, and related frameworks made this layer explicit by making it easier to instantiate agents, assign tools, control turn-taking, include humans, execute code, and route outputs [@autogen; @agentverse; @agentscope; @magenticone; @openhands; @autoagent]. @fig-autogen illustrates this conversation-programming view.

![AutoGen's conversation-programming abstraction connects conversable agents backed by LLMs, tools, code execution, and humans. The application defines the conversation pattern, including who can reply, when they reply, and which capabilities each agent can use. Reproduced from @autogen.](figures/autogen-conversation-programming.pdf){#fig-autogen width=92% fig-alt="AutoGen conversation programming diagram showing conversable agents connected through conversation patterns and backed by LLMs, tools, code execution, and humans."}

This reframing had two consequences. First, orchestration became the object of study. A multi-agent application could vary along dimensions such as centralized versus decentralized control, static versus dynamic membership, serial versus parallel execution, shared versus isolated memory, free-form versus structured messages, and human-in-the-loop versus fully automated operation. Second, the machinery of coordination became visible: not just who speaks next, but what state is saved, what tools are callable, what execution is sandboxed, what logs survive, and what evidence can be inspected later. Tool APIs, Docker sandboxes, event streams, file systems, queues, state stores, validators, ledgers, retry logic, permission boundaries, and benchmark harnesses matter as much as the model prompt.

The framework view also clarified a subtle problem: if everything is conversation, nothing is durable. A chat message can state that a task is done, but it does not by itself create a verifiable object. A reviewer can say a patch is correct, but that is weaker than a test log. A memory summary can claim that a user prefers a fact, but that is weaker than provenance and update history. The stronger systems therefore started to move from transient messages toward durable artifacts: plans, diffs, tests, retrieval traces, experiment logs, evaluation reports, memory records, and human approval events.

This infrastructure turn did not produce a single PyTorch for multi-agent systems. Most recent systems still hand-roll the coordination logic that matters most. CAID builds on OpenHands but contributes its own branch-and-merge protocol with isolated `git worktree`s, centralized task assignment, commits, merges, and verification [@caid]. Magentic-One builds on AutoGen but adds a ledger-driven orchestrator and tool-centric workers [@magenticone]. InternAgent uses Aider and OpenHands for code changes but hand-rolls a research loop around literature search, idea generation, assessment, experiment planning, and execution [@internagent]. Curie, AgentNet, MaAS, MemMA, CooperBench, DELEGATE-52, and SlopCodeBench define their own runtime or evaluation harnesses because their central claims depend on domain-specific state, artifacts, tools, or validators [@curie; @agentnet; @maas; @memma; @cooperbench; @delegate52; @slopcodebench].

The reason is structural. Deep-learning frameworks could standardize tensors, modules, gradients, losses, and optimizers. Multi-agent LLM systems have not converged on an equivalent computational object. The unit being composed may be a role prompt, a tool-using loop, a browser state, a code branch, a memory entry, an experiment, a debate trace, a verifier, or a human review. The common lesson is therefore not convergence on one framework. It is that serious multi-agent claims now depend on runtime contracts: isolation, state, tools, logs, permissions, verifiers, cost accounting, and artifact integration.

This transition also widened the comparison class. *More Agents Is All You Need* [@moreagents] and *Mixture-of-Agents* [@mixtureofagents] show that useful multi-agent inference may look less like dialogue and more like sampling, voting, feed-forward aggregation, and model diversity. These systems are important because they isolate a simpler mechanism: additional inference can help when independent candidates or heterogeneous models provide useful evidence to an aggregator. They also raise the standard for conversational multi-agent claims. If a complex role-play team beats a single call, it should also beat strong sampling, aggregation, and best-of-N baselines under comparable budgets.

As orchestration became easier to build, agent behavior became harder to defend with transcripts alone. A system could look impressive while losing state, calling the wrong tool, accepting a weak intermediate result, or leaving no durable evidence that the task was actually complete. The next pressure on the field came from executable tests of whether harnessed agents could change external state correctly.
